Précis

A claim-bounded complete reasoning record for Erdős #68. It retains the factorial-successor and carry normal forms, channel and projection mechanisms, exact finite denominator evidence, failed routes, and every registered family in the shared reader order. No cofinal divisibility-miss producer is proved, so irrationality remains open.

This paper owns the complete problem-specific reasoning surface for Erdős #68, including all registered result families and their boundaries.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #68, which remains open.

Which prime powers survive reduction

Problem 1 (Erdős #68). Is 𝑆 =∑𝑛≥2(𝑛! −1)−1S=∑n≥2(n!−1)−1 irrational?

Erdős states the question on p. 102 of his 1988 survey and, in the same passage, records the expectation that ∑𝑛1/(𝑛! +𝑡)∑n1/(n!+t) is irrational, indeed transcendental, for every integer 𝑡t [1]. That is conjectural context. Numbering and current status follow Bloom’s Erdős problem catalogue [2]; the problem is open.

Put

𝑑𝑛=𝑛!−1,𝐻𝑀=𝑀∑𝑛=21𝑑𝑛,𝐿𝑀=lcm⁡(𝑑2,…,𝑑𝑀),𝐴𝑀=𝑀∑𝑛=2𝐿𝑀𝑑𝑛,dn=n!−1,HM=∑n=2M1dn,LM=lcm⁡(d2,…,dM),AM=∑n=2MLMdn,

so that 𝐻𝑀 =𝐴𝑀/𝐿𝑀HM=AM/LM. Throughout, den⁡(𝑥)den⁡(x) is the positive denominator of a rational number in lowest terms. The first question is which prime power present in 𝐿𝑀LM remains in den⁡(𝐻𝑀)den⁡(HM).

Finally den⁡(𝐻𝑀) =𝐿𝑀/gcd(𝐴𝑀,𝐿𝑀)den⁡(HM)=LM/gcd(AM,LM), whose 𝑝p-valuation is 𝑒e exactly when 𝑝 ∤𝐴𝑀p∤AM. Since 𝑊W is invertible modulo 𝑝p, that is exactly the stated condition. ◻

The criterion decides the survival of the full exponent 𝑒e. A zero residue gives 𝑣𝑝(den⁡(𝐻𝑀)) <𝑒vp(den⁡(HM))<e, and further congruences are needed to determine the surviving exponent. The proof uses no property of factorials beyond the displayed denominators, so it applies to any finite sum of reciprocals. It is the first valuation layer of the reciprocal-sum formula of Louwsma and Martino [3]. What is specific here is the behaviour of the actual family 𝑑𝑛 =𝑛! −1dn=n!−1, and that behaviour is not generic.

A prime is prefix-private at 𝑚m when it divides 𝑑𝑚dm and divides none of 𝑑2,…,𝑑𝑚−1d2,…,dm−1.

Proposition 3 (cofinal first prime occurrences). For every integer 𝐵 ≥0B≥0 there are a prime 𝑞q and an integer 𝑚 >𝐵m>B with 𝑚 <𝑞m<q, 𝑞 ∣𝑚! −1q∣m!−1 and gcd(𝑞,𝑘! −1) =1gcd(q,k!−1)=1 for every 𝑘k with 2 ≤𝑘 <𝑚2≤k<m.

Proof. Choose a prime 𝑞 ≥𝐵! +5q≥B!+5. Wilson’s theorem gives (𝑞 −2)! ≡1(mod𝑞)(q−2)!≡1(modq), so the set of indices 𝑛 ≥2n≥2 with 𝑞 ∣𝑛! −1q∣n!−1 is nonempty and contains no element above 𝑞 −2q−2; let 𝑚m be its least element. If 𝑚 ≤𝐵m≤B, then 𝑞 ≤𝑚! −1 ≤𝐵! −1q≤m!−1≤B!−1, contradicting the choice of 𝑞q. Hence 𝑚 >𝐵m>B, and minimality gives the coprimality assertions. ◻

The construction gives no useful upper bound for 𝑞q in terms of its first hit, and that comparison is what the scale inequalities of §4 consume. Wilson reflection limits what can be inferred from a large prime factor alone: for odd 𝑛 <𝑞n<q with 𝑞 ∣𝑛! −1q∣n!−1, the identity (𝑞 −1 −𝑛)! 𝑛! ≡( −1)𝑛+1(mod𝑞)(q−1−n)!n!≡(−1)n+1(modq) gives a second hit at 𝑞 −𝑛 −1q−n−1. The reflection identity is classical; see Stewart [7].

The growth of the common denominator

Theorem 2 concerns the denominator after reduction. The common denominator before reduction admits an unconditional lower bound of its own, by an elementary argument.

The LCM asymptotic is proved here by an ordinary mathematical argument and is not kernel-checked. The associated asymptotic Lean files are proof candidates and are not being cited as kernel verification. The finite-block inequality has a separate Lean source, finite terminal-block inequality. Its two ingredients are Lemmas 4 and 5, and it needs no factorial-congruence multiplicity theorem. A weaker exponent 4/34/3 follows instead from Theorem 12 of Garaev, Luca and Shparlinski [6], which bounds by 𝑂(𝑁2/3)O(N2/3) the number of solutions of 𝑛! ≡𝑎(mod𝑟)n!≡a(modr) with 𝑟r prime, 𝑎 ≢0(mod𝑟)a≢0(modr), and 𝐻 +1 ≤𝑛 ≤𝐻 +𝑁H+1≤n≤H+N where 0 ≤𝐻 <𝐻 +𝑁 <𝑟0≤H<H+N<r; that deduction is recorded in the complete reasoning record and is superseded here. No antecedent for a lower bound on the least common multiple of the numbers 𝑛! −1n!−1 was located, and the searches were for factorial values shifted by one; least common multiples of consecutive integers and of linear recurrences are a different family. The finding is that the statement is possibly known and was not located.

The constant 2√2/322/3 is the best this argument gives. The gain from a block of 𝑘k indices is largest at the top of the range and the pairwise-gcd loss grows with the spread, so consecutive top indices are simultaneously optimal for both terms, and the bound 𝑗!/𝑖! <𝑁𝑗−𝑖j!/i!<Nj−i is sharp to first order there. Convergence is slow: the omitted term −𝑘𝑢−ku is of order 𝑁3/2N3/2, so the finite ratio falls short of the limit by about √2/log⁡𝑁2/log⁡N.

Theorem 7 is a statement about 𝐿𝑁LN and not about den⁡(𝐻𝑁)den⁡(HN). Consecutive denominators (𝑁 −1)! −1(N−1)!−1 and 𝑁! −1N!−1 are already coprime for 𝑁 ≥3N≥3, so the qualitative failure of common-denominator clearing follows from two terms; the estimate is the quantitative growth statement. Theorem 2 and the cancellations at 139139 and 25932593 show why the substitution fails: a prime may occupy the common denominator and be absent from the reduced one. One cancelled prime is not an asymptotic cancellation theorem.

The direction of denominator control matters. Write 𝐻𝑁 =𝐴𝑁/𝑄𝑁HN=AN/QN in lowest terms. Under the hypothetical identity 𝑆 =𝑎/𝑞S=a/q, with 𝑎 ∈ℤa∈Z and 𝑞 ≥1q≥1, positivity of the tail gives

𝑞𝑄𝑁(𝑆−𝐻𝑁)=𝑎𝑄𝑁−𝑞𝐴𝑁∈ℤ>0.qQN(S−HN)=aQN−qAN∈Z>0.

A direct clearing contradiction therefore requires an upper estimate that makes 𝑞𝑄𝑁(𝑆 −𝐻𝑁) <1qQN(S−HN)<1 for some 𝑁N; equivalently, it needs 𝑄𝑁QN to be small relative to the reciprocal tail. A lower bound on 𝑄𝑁QN points in the opposite direction. Indeed, the rational limit 11 and the approximants 1 −1/𝑄𝑁1−1/QN have arbitrarily large reduced denominators without any irrationality. The inequality 𝑑𝑁(𝑆 −𝐻𝑁) <1dN(S−HN)<1 alone would not repair the argument, because 𝑑𝑁dN generally does not clear the earlier summands of 𝐻𝑁HN. The prime-pole analysis describes which factors survive reduction, but it does not yet supply the required upper control on 𝑄𝑁QN.

Why one proposed window argument is circular

One route to cofinal non-unit carries tries to exclude two consecutive unit carries by extracting a prime-power or quotient-gcd obstruction from their cleared width-one window. The exact two-step recurrence shows what that window can deliver. Let 𝑈𝑘Uk and 𝑉𝑘Vk be the numerator and denominator of the reduced predecessor gap and let 𝐺𝑘 >0Gk>0 be the exact transition normaliser. For 𝑚 ≥3m≥3, the two unit carries are equivalent to an integer offset Ω𝑚Ωm with 0 <Ω𝑚 ≤𝐷𝑚0<Ωm≤Dm, the window denominator telescopes independently of the carry values,

𝐷𝑚=𝑉𝑚+2𝐺𝑚+1𝐺𝑚=𝑉𝑚(𝑚!−1)((𝑚+1)!−1),Dm=Vm+2Gm+1Gm=Vm(m!−1)((m+1)!−1),

and under the pair assumption the offset factors to match, Ω𝑚 =𝑈𝑚+2𝐺𝑚+1𝐺𝑚Ωm=Um+2Gm+1Gm. Cancelling the common positive normaliser reduces the complete window to

0<𝑈𝑚+2≤𝑉𝑚+2,0<Um+2≤Vm+2,

which every reduced positive gap in (0,1](0,1] already satisfies. For that specified window, therefore, an obstruction obtained only after imposing the carry pair rewrites a bound that holds anyway. The calculation does not disprove adjacent unit carries and does not exclude an independent restriction on the transition numerators or their valuations, which would need its own argument constraining the predecessor state before the pair is assumed.

At zero cost in the moment this supplies a unit in the 𝑝p-channel: adding an integer multiple of the corrector to any candidate kernel shifts the 𝑝p-channel by multiples of 𝑝! −1p!−1 and leaves the moment and every other channel fixed. For every channel rank and every prescribed cutoff there is a factorial-grid kernel together with a remote prime-corrector pair entirely beyond that cutoff, with all requested low channels zero, nonzero moment, and residual in [ −1/2,1/2][−1/2,1/2]. Finite denominator exclusions

Two finite computations constrain a hypothetical denominator 𝑞q in 𝑆 =𝑎/𝑞S=a/q, and they constrain different features of it:

𝑞∤299999!,𝑞≥239990>1012038.(22)(22)q∤299999!,q≥239990>1012038.

The size bound holds for every integer 𝑎a and positive natural 𝑞q with 𝑆 =𝑎/𝑞S=a/q; no reducedness assumption is needed. Its evidence is the exact continued-fraction computation described below. The stronger candidate finite-size Lean certificate is not cited as kernel verification: its source records that the computation has not yet been kernel checked. The factorial-grid exclusion 𝑞 ∤299999!q∤299999! is supported separately by the external GMP computation; its full Lean certificate also remains an outstanding formal obligation.

Neither implies the other. A denominator with no prime factor above 299999299999 can still fail to divide 299999!299999! by carrying one prime to a high power, and a denominator far below 239990239990 can still fail that divisibility; a magnitude bound above 299999!299999! would imply it, and no such bound is available here.

The remaining arithmetic inputs

Prove long68:eq:finite-escape at arbitrarily large indices; restricting to primes is sufficient. The upper alternative is exactly ((𝑚 +2)𝑚! −2)𝑣𝑚 ≤𝑚2(𝑚! −1)𝑢𝑚((m+2)m!−2)vm≤m2(m!−1)um. Criteria from the literature that do not apply.

Duverney’s fast-series criteria assume two-sided quadratic denominator growth 𝑐𝑢2𝑛 ≤𝑢𝑛+1 ≤𝑐′𝑢2𝑛cun2≤un+1≤c′un2, whereas 𝑢𝑛+1/𝑢2𝑛 →0un+1/un2→0 for 𝑢𝑛 =𝑛! −1un=n!−1, and his all-positive specialisation additionally requires ∑𝑛|𝑢𝑛+1/𝑢2𝑛 −1| <∞∑n|un+1/un2−1|<∞, whose summands tend to one here [9]. The theorem of Barreto, Kang, Kim, Kovač and Zhang proves irrationality of ∑𝑛1/𝑎𝑛∑n1/an under a rapid-growth hypothesis that fails for 𝑎𝑛 =𝑛! −1an=n!−1, since log⁡(𝑛! −1) =𝑂(𝑛log⁡𝑛)log⁡(n!−1)=O(nlog⁡n) makes (𝑛! −1)1/𝜓𝑛 →1(n!−1)1/ψn→1 for every fixed 𝜓 >1ψ>1 . Failure of a sufficient criterion is not a theorem about 𝑆S, and the useful content is the target these papers identify: a low-height clearing subsequence, or enough exact cancellation in the least common multiple. Theorem 7 bounds that cancellation from one side and Theorem 2 describes it from the other.

Erdős #68 is open. Every rational representation with positive denominator has 𝑞 ≥300000q≥300000.

Attribution. Wilson’s theorem and the Wilson reflection identity are classical, the latter recorded by Stewart [7]. The factorial-digit termination criterion is Cantor’s [4], in the form recorded by Galambos ; the additions here are the telescope 𝐶 =𝑆 −𝑒 +2C=S−e+2, the identification of the digit value 𝑚 −2m−2, and the transport to the shifted family. The multiplicity bound is Garaev, Luca and Shparlinski’s , and the lcm deduction from it is not theirs. The survival criterion is a specialisation of Louwsma and Martino’s valuation formula . For the Wilson cofinality packaging, the finite radius bound and Theorem 7, no antecedent was located, which is a negative search result, and no priority is claimed.

Extended record

The short note above carries the advertised results with complete proofs. This part keeps the surrounding mathematics: the digit kernel the carry and orbit criteria run on, the exact interfaces of the collision-core reduction, the finite certificates, the superseded deductions, and the routes that were tried and closed.

Criteria from the literature, in full

Koepf and Schmersau prove that eventual equality between the floors of 𝑛n times a partial sum and 𝑛n times its limit forces irrationality [8]; their rational-term version obtains that equality from prefix integrality at a scale 𝑝𝑛pn together with the strict tail bound 𝑎 −𝑠𝑛 <1/(𝑛𝑝𝑛)a−sn<1/(npn) . For the natural termwise clearing choice 𝑝𝑛 =lcm⁡{𝑘! −1 :2 ≤𝑘 ≤𝑛}pn=lcm⁡{k!−1:2≤k≤n} the last two denominators already obstruct it:

𝑝𝑛 ≥ (𝑛!−1)((𝑛−1)!−1)𝑛−1,pn ≥ (n!−1)((n−1)!−1)n−1,

because gcd(𝑛! −1,(𝑛 −1)! −1) =gcd((𝑛 −1)! −1,𝑛 −1) ≤𝑛 −1gcd(n!−1,(n−1)!−1)=gcd((n−1)!−1,n−1)≤n−1. For 𝑛 ≥4n≥4 the first omitted summand 1/((𝑛 +1)! −1)1/((n+1)!−1) then already exceeds 1/(𝑛𝑝𝑛)1/(npn), so this 𝑝𝑛pn cannot satisfy their tail hypothesis. Cancellation in the reduced prefix denominator could give a smaller scale, and proving enough cancellation is another form of the present denominator problem.

Duverney’s Theorem 3.1 assumes two-sided quadratic denominator growth 𝑐𝑢2𝑛 ≤𝑢𝑛+1 ≤𝑐′𝑢2𝑛cun2≤un+1≤c′un2, while 𝑢𝑛+1/𝑢2𝑛 →0un+1/un2→0 for 𝑢𝑛 =𝑛! −1un=n!−1 [9]; his all-positive Corollary 3.2 additionally requires ∑𝑛|𝑢𝑛+1/𝑢2𝑛 −1| <∞∑n|un+1/un2−1|<∞, whereas those summands tend to one [9]. Both the ratio limit and the nonsummability are kernel-checked. The ratio proof divides numerator and denominator by (𝑛!)2(n!)2; the resulting terms tend to zero while (1 −1/𝑛!)2(1−1/n!)2 tends to one.

The theorem of Barreto, Kang, Kim, Kovač and Zhang proves irrationality of ∑𝑛1/𝑎𝑛∑n1/an when 𝑎1/2𝑛𝑛 →∞an1/2n→∞, whereas (𝑛! −1)1/2𝑛 →1(n!−1)1/2n→1 [11]; the limit is kernel-checked through the bound 0 ≤log⁡(𝑛! −1) ≤𝑛20≤log⁡(n!−1)≤n2. Their proof identifies a useful exact criterion: Mahler’s elementary rationality floor is contradicted by prefix-clearing integers 𝐷𝑁DN whose cleared positive tails satisfy lim inf𝑁𝐷𝑁𝑟𝑁 =0lim infNDNrN=0 . The primitive lcm divisibility survives cofactor removal: factorial valuations do not remove the channel obstruction once every common cofactor divisor has been removed. A corank-one cofactor and determinant construction for such primitive kernels has not been formalised, and the divisibility theorem does not establish it.

If 𝑟r is prime, 𝑒 >0e>0 and 𝑟𝑒 ∣˜𝐶𝑝re∣C~p, there are 𝑖 <𝑗i<j in 𝐼𝑝Ip with 𝑟𝑒+𝑣𝑟(𝐹𝑝) ∣𝑖! −1re+vr(Fp)∣i!−1, 𝑟𝑒+𝑣𝑟(𝐹𝑝) ∣𝑗! −1re+vr(Fp)∣j!−1 and 𝑟𝑒+𝑣𝑟(𝐹𝑝) ≤𝑗𝑗−𝑖re+vr(Fp)≤jj−i; consequently (2𝑝 −1)𝑑 <𝑟𝑒+𝑣𝑟(𝐹𝑝)(2p−1)d<re+vr(Fp) forces 𝑑 <𝑗 −𝑖d<j−i. The spacing hypothesis is discharged internally: any two 𝑟𝑒re-hits 𝑖 <𝑗i<j satisfy 𝑒 <𝑗 −𝑖e<j−i, because 𝑟 ∣𝑗! −1r∣j!−1 already forces 𝑗 <𝑟j<r and the gap-power inequality converts that size relation into strict separation. The pairwise form is stronger than the selected-witness form: for arbitrary 𝑟,𝑒r,e and any displayed hits 𝑖 <𝑗i<j,

𝑟𝑒∣𝑖!−1,𝑟𝑒∣𝑗!−1⟹𝑟𝑒≤𝑗𝑗−𝑖,re∣i!−1,re∣j!−1⟹re≤jj−i,

so every prime-power hit layer is an 𝑒e-separated subset of the block and

The unweighted packing step is therefore complete. Globally,

𝑟∣˜𝐶𝑝⟹𝑣𝑟(˜𝐶𝑝)+𝑣𝑟(𝐹𝑝)<2𝑝−3r∣C~p⟹vr(C~p)+vr(Fp)<2p−3

What remains is to bound the layer counts uniformly as 𝑟r and 𝑝p move, multiply the surviving contributions, and still close the complementary-residue coordinate.

The squarefreeness premise is not proved. An exhaustive modular scan through 𝑟 ≤2,000,000r≤2,000,000 and 𝑛 ≤240n≤240 found four individual square hits and no prime with two such hits. All 498,501498,501 pairs 2 ≤𝑎 <𝑏 ≤10002≤a<b≤1000 have squarefree gcd(𝑎! −1,𝑏! −1)gcd(a!−1,b!−1), and the aggregate squarefree-collision scan through 𝑝 =499p=499 stays below 0.3740.374 of the upper-descending-factorial logarithmic scale. These are finite exact computations. They carry neither theorem authority nor an asymptotic incidence bound.

A finite variant of the cofinal private supply compares the product of a chosen set of primes, each at least 55, with ∏2≤𝑘≤𝐵(𝑘! −1)∏2≤k≤B(k!−1); if the prime product is larger, at least one chosen prime has no hit through 𝐵B, while Wilson still bounds its least hit by 𝑞 −2q−2. Wilson reflection limits what a linear-size divisor can be assumed to be: if 𝑛n is odd, 𝑛 <𝑞n<q, and 𝑞 ∣𝑛! −1q∣n!−1, then 𝑞 ∣(𝑞 −𝑛 −1)! −1q∣(q−n−1)!−1, and when both indices lie in one block with the reflected hit earlier, equivalently 𝑞 <2𝑛 +1q<2n+1, the repeated hit survives predecessor-factorial normalisation and its full-block incidence count exceeds one.

Stewart states that for every 𝜀 >0ε>0 there are infinitely many odd 𝑛n whose least prime factor 𝑞q of 𝑛! −1n!−1 satisfies

𝑛<𝑞<(√145−18+𝜀)𝑛,n<q<(145−18+ε)n,

the printed text transferring estimate (9) from 𝑛! +1n!+1 to 𝑛! −1n!−1 [7]. The source controls 𝑞q relative to the later index 𝑛n and supplies no control relative to the private first-hit index, so it is collision-core input. The missing private-anchor and global product estimates are elsewhere.

One selected prime 𝑞q already furnishes the coprime factor pair (1,𝑞)(1,q): its projection moduli are 𝑅𝑝Rp and 𝑅𝑝/𝑞Rp/q, whose least common multiple is 𝑅𝑝Rp, so no second selected prime is needed and there is no hidden equality-or-disagreement branch in that specialisation. The underlying projection rigidity is general: if the endpoint numerator 𝑍Z is congruent to a weighted numerator 𝑇T modulo 𝑅R, then every divisor 𝑄Q of 𝑅R with 𝑍 ≤𝐵 <𝑄Z≤B<Q satisfies 𝑇mod𝑄 =𝑍TmodQ=Z, so two divisors above 𝐵B with unequal projected residues exclude that bounded endpoint, and unequal projections force min(𝑄1,𝑄2) ≤𝑇min(Q1,Q2)≤T.

Limits of fixed-coordinate arguments

  • Residue vectors, their recurrences, and window widths admit synthetic all-hit blocks, so they cannot prove irrationality on their own.

  • Known pointwise prime congruences, prime-dilation congruences, parity, and the exact prime coefficient formula admit a synthetic rational countermodel.

  • Wilson quotients, harmonic sums, 𝑝p-adic gamma identities, and factorial residues do not control the required Archimedean floor without an additional coupling theorem. Every prime-window test factors into a sharp Archimedean strict-ceiling condition and a modular divisibility condition, and the missing ingredient is the coupling between them.

  • Fixed-denominator scalar canonical-product localisers and rank-saturated consecutive-jet Hermite–Padé systems pay the full factorial-gap denominator. For 𝐸(𝑧) =∏𝑛≥2(1 −𝑧/𝑛!)E(z)=∏n≥2(1−z/n!) the genus-zero product satisfies −𝐸′(1)/𝐸(1) =𝑆−E′(1)/E(1)=S, and the natural scalar linear form carries the coefficient 𝑄𝑁 =∏2≤𝑛≤𝑁(𝑛! −1)QN=∏2≤n≤N(n!−1), for which 𝑄𝑁QN times the tail diverges. Exact first-order interpolation, scalar residue weighting, the natural Wronskian, and rank-saturated consecutive jets all reassemble the same prohibitive denominator.

  • Zero-moment variations cannot create an additional fractional cancellation coordinate, and factorial valuations cannot absorb the channel lcm obstruction.

  • A fixed pair of low-index private owners cannot make the projection argument cofinal, by the absorption statement of the short note.

The generic shape behind the lower-interval form

The cofinal statement in the short note has a generic ancestor. For a real 𝑥x and any positive sequence 𝑐𝑚cm with 𝑐𝑚 <1/𝑚cm<1/m eventually,

𝑥∉ℚ⟺{(𝑚−1)!𝑥}≥𝑐𝑚 for arbitrarily large 𝑚.x∉Q⟺{(m−1)!x}≥cm for arbitrarily large m.

For rational 𝑥x the fractional parts vanish eventually; if all large fractional parts lie below 𝑐𝑚cm, multiplying by 𝑚m stays below one, so the next canonical digit is zero, and eventual zero digits force rationality. The specific target 𝑐𝑚 =𝐸𝑚/𝑚cm=Em/m is useful because it translates into finite predecessor-gap conditions. The smallness of the target alone establishes no metric, measure or equidistribution theorem for this orbit, and none is claimed.
